hub.title: Who Slate is for: Indian food, home cooking, eating out
hub.description: How to count calories in Indian food at home, at the office, eating out and on fasting days, in Hinglish, without a login. Written by the makers of Slate.
intro: Slate is a calorie journal for people who eat Indian food: home dal and roti, a canteen thali, a Swiggy order and chai, often all in the same week. These pages explain how to count each of them honestly, and where Slate helps.
Every number on these pages comes from the food pages in [Calories in Indian food](/calories/), which show their recipes, arithmetic and sources.

pages.title: Calorie counter for Indian food: katori, roti and oil
pages.description: Why calorie apps struggle with dal, roti and sabzi, what an honest number for Indian food needs, and how Slate counts by your katori, roti and oil.
pages.h1: A calorie counter for Indian food
pages.linkLabel: A calorie counter for Indian food
pages.lede: Indian food is counted by the katori, the roti and the spoon of oil, and the same dal can have twice the calories in one home as in another. A calorie counter for Indian food has to start from those things, not from a database of packaged foods.

body.h2: Why Indian food is hard to count
content: Most of what Indians eat is cooked at home or bought freshly made, so there's no label. The same dish name also covers very different food. A 200 ml katori of thin [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/) has about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} calories, while the same katori of thicker [dal fry](/calories/dal-fry/) has about {{kcal@dal-fry:k200}}. Both are "a katori of dal".

Katoris themselves differ. A 150 ml katori of dal tadka is about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k150}} calories and a 250 ml one about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k250}}. Rotis differ too: a phulka made from about 24 g of atta is about {{kcal@roti:phulka}}, a large roti from 40 g about {{kcal@roti:large}}.

Then there's oil. A teaspoon of oil or ghee is about 40 to 45 calories, and home cooks use very different amounts. Restaurant food usually carries more again: a home bowl of [paneer butter masala](/calories/paneer-butter-masala/) with 50 g of paneer is about {{kcal@paneer-butter-masala:bowl}} calories, and a restaurant serving about {{outLo@paneer-butter-masala}} to {{outHi@paneer-butter-masala}}.

body.h2: What an honest number for Indian food needs
content: A number you can rely on, day after day, comes from a few plain things:

ul: A recipe in grams, so you know how much atta, dal, oil and ghee went into the dish.
Values for Indian ingredients as they're grown and sold here, from the ICMR-NIN Indian Food Composition Tables 2017 (IFCT 2017).
Portions in household measures, such as a katori, a roti, a plate or a glass, rather than grams you'd need to weigh.
The size of your own katori and roti, and how much oil your family uses.
Whether it was cooked at home or outside. Restaurant, delivery and street food usually have more oil and bigger portions.

content: IFCT 2017 lists raw ingredients, not cooked dishes, so every dish has to be worked out from a recipe. That's what the [food calorie pages](/calories/) on this site do, with each recipe and source shown.

body.h2: How to count Indian food better, with or without an app

ol: Measure your everyday katori once with water and a measuring jug. Knowing whether it's 150, 200 or 250 ml changes most of your numbers.
Count rotis, not plates. Two medium rotis are about {{kcal@roti:two}} calories; the dal and sabzi are separate.
Notice the fat. A teaspoon of ghee on a roti, an extra tadka or a cube of butter on a paratha is often the biggest difference between two similar meals.
Treat outside food as outside. A dhaba dal or a delivery biryani isn't the same as yours at home.
Accept a range. Every calorie number is an estimate. Being consistent matters more than being exact.

content: Slate is a calorie journal for iPhone built around these facts. You type a line the way you'd say it, "2 roti aur ek katori dal", and Slate puts a number next to it.

The number is worked out on your phone from IFCT 2017 values and dish recipes in grams, then adjusted for your kitchen: your katori (150, 200 or 250 ml), your roti (6, 8 or 10 inches), your oil, and the sugar and milk in your chai. Restaurant, delivery, street and canteen food is counted as outside food, with more oil and a bigger portion, and you can switch any line to "Made at home". Tap any number to see how it was worked out, ingredient by ingredient.
AI is used only to read a line Slate doesn't recognise, and it never produces a calorie number. If Slate can't recognise a line at all, it shows a grey ↻ and counts it as zero rather than guessing.

Slate doesn't suggest a goal, a diet or a target weight, and it never praises eating less or comments on eating more. It's a journal and a set of numbers, not a coach. It's for adults, it's not medical advice, and it's on iPhone only.

faq.q: How many calories are in a typical Indian thali?
faq.a: Add up what's on it. Two medium [rotis](/calories/roti/) are about {{kcal@roti:two}}, a 200 ml katori of [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/) about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}}, a katori of [aloo sabzi](/calories/aloo-sabzi/) about {{kcal@aloo-sabzi:k200}} and a 200 ml katori of [rice](/calories/plain-rice/) about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}}. Ghee, papad and pickle add more.

faq.q: Are calorie numbers for Indian food accurate?
faq.a: They're estimates, as every calorie number is. Recipes, katoris and oil vary from home to home, so the honest answer is often a range. Using the same method every day matters more than any single number being exact.

faq.q: Does IFCT 2017 list cooked Indian dishes?
faq.a: No. The ICMR-NIN Indian Food Composition Tables 2017 list ingredients such as atta, dal, vegetables, milk and oils. Cooked dishes have to be worked out from a recipe in grams.

faq.q: Is Slate a calorie counter for Indian food?
faq.a: Yes, written as a journal. You type what you ate the way you'd say it, in English or Hinglish, and Slate counts the calories, protein, carbs and fat for each line using Indian food composition data.

pages.title: Calorie counting for vegetarians, including Jain food
pages.description: Counting calories and protein in vegetarian and Jain meals: dal, paneer, curd, chana and besan, with katori-by-katori numbers from IFCT 2017.
pages.h1: Calorie counting for vegetarians, including Jain food
pages.lede: For vegetarians, the useful numbers are usually protein and fat as much as calories: how much protein a katori of dal really gives, and how quickly paneer, ghee and fried snacks add up. Jain cooking changes the vegetables, but the oil and the dairy decide most of the calories.

content: In a vegetarian Indian diet, protein comes mostly from dal, beans, paneer, curd, milk and besan. Cooked dal is mostly water, so a katori holds less than people expect:

ul: A bowl of plain [toor dal](/calories/toor-dal/) made from 30 g of dry dal has about {{protein@toor-dal:bowl}} g of protein.
A 200 ml katori of [rajma](/calories/rajma/) has about {{protein@rajma:k200}} g, and of [chole](/calories/chole/) about {{protein@chole:k200}} g.
A home bowl of [palak paneer](/calories/palak-paneer/) with 40 g of paneer has about {{protein@palak-paneer:bowl}} g.
Two [besan chillas](/calories/besan-chilla/) have about {{protein@besan-chilla:two}} g.

content: Raw toor dal has 21.7 g of protein per 100 g and paneer 18.9 g, according to IFCT 2017, but you eat dal cooked and diluted and paneer in small cubes. Counting by what's in your katori is more useful than counting by the packet.
Vegetarian food isn't automatically light or heavy. The same few things make the difference in most meals:

ul: Paneer is about {{ing:paneer}} calories per 100 g. A restaurant serving often has two or three times the paneer of a home katori.
Each teaspoon of ghee or oil is about 40 to 45 calories, whether it's in the tadka, on the roti or in the kadhai.
Fried snacks add up quickly: a home [samosa](/calories/samosa/) is about {{kcal@samosa:one}} calories and two [medu vadas](/calories/medu-vada/) about {{kcal@medu-vada:two}}.
So do sweets and sweet drinks: a home [gulab jamun](/calories/gulab-jamun/) is about {{kcal@gulab-jamun:one}} calories and a glass of [sweet lassi](/calories/lassi/) about {{kcal@lassi:glass}}.

content: Jain cooking leaves out onion, garlic, potato and other root vegetables, and many Jain families don't eat after sunset. Taking out onion and garlic changes a dish's calories very little: 25 g of onion is about 12 calories. The oil, ghee, dairy and sugar decide the number, as they do in any vegetarian kitchen.
Where potato is replaced with raw banana or another vegetable, count that vegetable instead. Dal, kadhi, rotis, theplas and most sabzis can be counted the same way, by the katori and the roti.

body.h2: How to count a vegetarian day

ol: Count dal by the dry dal when you cook it, or by the katori when you serve it, and keep to one katori size.
Count paneer, curd and milk separately when you can. They carry most of the protein and much of the fat.
Count ghee and oil you add at the table: a teaspoon on rice, dal or roti.
Count fried snacks and sweets as their own lines, not as part of the meal.

content: In Slate you can tell it your diet: vegetarian, eggetarian, non-vegetarian, vegan or Jain, and the foods you avoid. That helps Slate read your lines the way you mean them. Every line shows protein, carbs and fat as well as calories, and you can set macro goals yourself; Slate never suggests one.
Write "1 katori rajma, 2 roti, dahi" and each part gets its own line and its own number, adjusted for your katori, roti and oil.

faq.q: How much protein is in a katori of dal?
faq.a: A bowl of plain toor dal made from 30 g of dry dal has about {{protein@toor-dal:bowl}} g of protein. A thick dal, rajma or chole has more per katori: about {{protein@rajma:k200}} g in a 200 ml katori of rajma.

faq.q: Is Jain food lower in calories?
faq.a: Not by itself. Leaving out onion and garlic removes very few calories. Oil, ghee, dairy and sugar decide most of the number, in Jain cooking as in any other.

faq.q: How many calories are in 100 g of paneer?
faq.a: About {{ing:paneer}}, with about 18.9 g of protein and 14.8 g of fat, according to IFCT 2017.

faq.q: Can I track protein in Slate?
faq.a: Yes. Every line shows protein, carbs and fat, and macro goals are free. Slate doesn't suggest what your goals should be.

pages.title: Counting calories in home-cooked food: katori, roti, oil
pages.description: Three things decide the calories in home-cooked Indian food: your katori, your roti and your oil. How to measure each once, with numbers from IFCT 2017.
pages.lede: In home-cooked Indian food, three things decide most of the number: the size of your katori, the size of your roti and how much oil your family uses. Measure each of them once and your daily counting gets much closer to what you actually eat.

content: Katoris in Indian homes range from about 150 ml to 250 ml, and that alone changes a katori of dal or sabzi by two thirds. A 150 ml katori of [rajma](/calories/rajma/) is about {{kcal@rajma:k150}} calories and a 250 ml one about {{kcal@rajma:k250}}.
To measure yours, fill it with water to where you usually serve, and pour it into a measuring jug. Do it once for the katori you use most.

A roti's calories follow its atta, whatever its size when rolled out. A [phulka](/calories/phulka/) from about 24 g of atta is about {{kcal@phulka:one}} calories, a medium [roti](/calories/roti/) from 30 g about {{kcal@roti:medium}}, and a large one from 40 g about {{kcal@roti:large}}.

If you want to know your own, weigh a dough ball once on a kitchen scale. Dough is atta plus water, so a 50 g ball is roughly 30 g of atta. A teaspoon of ghee on top adds about 45 calories, close to half a roti.

Oil and ghee are where home kitchens differ most, and they're the hardest to see once a dish is cooked. Each teaspoon is about 40 to 45 calories. In a textbook [plain paratha](/calories/plain-paratha/), the oil is close to half the calories; in [bhindi sabzi](/calories/bhindi/), close to three quarters.

The easiest way to know your family's oil is the bottle. If a 1 litre bottle lasts about 30 days for 4 people, that's about 7.7 g of oil per person per day, or about 68 calories, spread across everything cooked at home.

body.h2: Thick or thin, home or outside
content: Dal, sambar and kadhi change with how much water they're cooked in. A 200 ml katori of thin [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/) is about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} calories, and a thick dal can be close to twice that. When you can, count dal by the dry dal that went into the pot: ICMR-NIN's standard serving is 30 g of dry dal.
Food cooked outside usually has more oil and a bigger portion, so count it separately: see [eating out](/for/eating-out/).

Slate asks for these once, in Your kitchen: your katori (150, 200 or 250 ml), your roti (6, 8 or 10 inches), your oil as a sentence such as "A 1 litre bottle lasts us about 30 days, cooking for 4 people", and the sugar and milk in your chai and coffee. It turns the oil into oil per person per day and spreads it across home-cooked dishes.

You can also add a short note on how you cook, such as "We cook with less oil than most. I use a small katori." Slate turns it into small, capped adjustments. Your kitchen is free, and changing it later never rewrites past days.

faq.q: How do I count calories in home-cooked food?
faq.a: Know your katori size, your roti size and roughly how much oil your family uses. Then count dishes by the katori and rotis by the piece, and add ghee or oil you put on at the table.

faq.q: How many calories does a teaspoon of oil add?
faq.a: About 40 calories for a teaspoon of oil (4.5 g) and about 45 for a teaspoon of ghee (5 g), from IFCT 2017.

faq.q: How do I measure my katori?
faq.a: Fill it with water to your usual serving level and pour it into a measuring jug. Most katoris are between 150 and 250 ml.

faq.q: How much oil does my family use per person?
faq.a: Divide the bottle by the days and the people. A 1 litre bottle lasting 30 days for 4 people is about 7.7 g, or 68 calories, per person per day.

pages.title: Calories in restaurant, Swiggy and Zomato food
pages.description: Why restaurant and delivery food has more calories than home food, with ranges for dal makhani, paneer, biryani and naan, and how to count an order.
pages.h1: Calories in restaurant, Swiggy and Zomato food
pages.linkLabel: Calories in restaurant and delivery food
pages.lede: Restaurant and delivery food usually has more calories than the same dish at home, mostly because of more butter, cream and oil and bigger portions. The honest way to count it is as a range, dish by dish.

content: Restaurant kitchens cook for taste and for portions that look generous. That usually means more ghee, butter and cream than a home kitchen uses, oil that's been used many times for frying, and bigger servings. None of it is printed on a menu, so the same dish can vary a lot from one place to the next.

Lab studies of street food in Delhi found samosas and kachoris with far more fat than home versions. A home [samosa](/calories/samosa/) is about {{kcal@samosa:one}} calories; the street samosas measured came to about {{outLo@samosa}} to {{outHi@samosa}}.
These ranges come from the food pages on this site, each worked out from a recipe in grams with its assumptions stated:

table.caption: Home value against a typical restaurant or delivery range. See each dish's page for how it was worked out.
head: Dish
Home
Restaurant or delivery

ol: Count each dish as its own line: the curry, the naans, the rice, the raita.
Use the restaurant range, not the home number. If you don't know, the middle of the range is a fair guess.
Count breads by the piece. A large restaurant naan is about three times a home naan before any butter goes on.
If you share, count your share: half a plate of biryani is half the number.
Don't forget drinks and sides: a sweet lassi, a gulab jamun, papad.

content: In Slate, every line can be switched between "Outside" and "Made at home". Outside food, from restaurants, delivery, street stalls and canteens, is counted with more oil and a bigger portion than home food, and dishes usually eaten out, like chole bhature, pav bhaji and biryani, count as outside unless you switch them.

With Slate Plus, you can share a Swiggy or Zomato order to Slate or paste it into a new line. The order text is read on your iPhone, fees and totals are dropped, and each dish becomes its own line, counted as outside food. You check the list and tap Add. Slate never connects to those apps.

faq.q: Why does restaurant food have more calories than home food?
faq.a: Mostly more butter, cream and oil, and bigger portions. Fried food from shops is often fried in oil that's used many times, which leaves more fat in each piece.

faq.q: How many calories are in a Swiggy biryani?
faq.a: No app can know a specific restaurant's recipe. As a range, a restaurant plate of [chicken biryani](/calories/chicken-biryani/) is about {{outLo@chicken-biryani}} to {{outHi@chicken-biryani}} calories, depending on the ghee and the size.

faq.q: How many calories are in a restaurant naan?
faq.a: A large plain restaurant [naan](/calories/naan/) is about {{kcal@naan:large}}, and a large [butter naan](/calories/butter-naan/) about {{kcal@butter-naan:large}}.

faq.q: Can Slate read my Swiggy or Zomato order?
faq.a: Yes, with Slate Plus. Share or paste the order to Slate, check the list, and each dish is added as outside food. Slate only reads what you share and never connects to those apps.

pages.description: Write "2 roti aur ek katori dal" or "chai, kam cheeni" and get a number. How Slate reads Hinglish and Gujarati spellings, and what it does when it can't.
pages.h1: A calorie tracker you can write in Hinglish
pages.linkLabel: A calorie tracker you can write in Hinglish
pages.lede: Most of us don't describe our food in database terms. We say "2 roti aur ek katori dal", "chai, kam cheeni" or "aadha plate poha". A calorie tracker that understands how you'd say it is quicker to use, and you're more likely to keep using it.

body.h2: Why typing it the way you'd say it helps
content: Searching a database for every item, choosing from ten kinds of dal and guessing a weight in grams takes time, and that's where most people stop logging. Writing one line, the way you'd tell a friend what you ate, takes seconds.
It also keeps the things that change the number: "kam tel", "extra ghee", "half plate" and "bina cheeni" are exactly the details a database search leaves out.
The same dish also has different names in different homes: rotli, phulka and chapati; shaak and sabzi; dahi and curd. A tracker that knows only one spelling makes you search for the others.

body.h2: What a line can look like

table.caption: Examples of lines and what they mean. Numbers are this site's home values, before your own kitchen settings.

It means

rows: 1 cup of chai with less sugar

content: Slate understands English, Hinglish and Gujarati-English spellings, quantities in words such as ek, do, aadha and half, and preparation words such as "less oil", "kam tel", "no sugar", "bina cheeni", "extra ghee", "half plate" and "full plate". One line can become several: "2 roti aur ek katori dal" becomes "2 roti" and "1 katori dal", each with its own number.

Slate's own matcher on your iPhone reads most lines. Only when it doesn't recognise one does AI help read it, and even then it can only point to dishes in Slate's own catalogue. The AI never produces a calorie number: the number is always worked out from food composition data and recipes in grams.

With Slate Plus you can also say the line instead of typing it, in English or Hinglish. Speech is turned into text on your iPhone, or by Apple's speech service where needed, and Slate never receives or stores audio.
If Slate can't recognise a line, it shows a grey ↻ and counts it as zero. It never guesses a number. You can rewrite the line, or tap it to choose the dish.
The app itself is in English for now. Writing in Hinglish and Gujarati spellings works; the menus and settings are in English.

faq.q: Can I write my food in Hinglish?
faq.a: Yes. Lines such as "2 roti aur ek katori dal", "kam tel" and "bina cheeni" work in Slate, along with Gujarati spellings.

faq.q: Does Slate understand Gujarati?
faq.a: Gujarati-English spellings such as "rotli", "shaak" and "dal bhaat" work. The app itself is in English for now.

faq.q: What happens if Slate doesn't understand a line?
faq.a: It shows a grey ↻ and counts the line as zero. It never guesses a number.

faq.q: Does AI decide the calories?
faq.a: No. AI is used only to read lines Slate doesn't recognise, and it can only point to dishes in Slate's catalogue. The number is worked out from food composition data and recipes in grams.

content: When you install Slate, it creates an anonymous account on your phone. You don't give a name, phone number or email, and Slate doesn't collect your contacts, your location or an advertising ID.
You open the app and start writing. There's no sign-up form, no verification code and no password to remember.

ul: Your Slate (the lines you write and their numbers) is stored in Mumbai, India, on Supabase servers in AWS's Mumbai region. Each account can read only its own data.
No ads, no ad SDKs, no tracking and no analytics at launch.
Barcode scanning sends only the barcode number to Open Food Facts. Label scanning happens on your phone.
When Slate doesn't recognise a line, the line is sent to Anthropic's AI to read. With Slate Plus, photos and chat messages are too. None of it is used to train AI models, and photos are never stored.
Subscriptions are handled by Apple, and RevenueCat holds only your subscription status.

content: Slate doesn't ask about health conditions or medication. Reminders, if you turn them on, are scheduled on your iPhone itself, with no push service and no marketing messages. And without a login there's nothing for a sales team to call or email; Slate doesn't have one.

content: Whichever app you use, these questions tell you most of what you need to know about your data:

ol: Do I need an account, and what does it ask for?
What's collected besides what I log, such as contacts, location or an advertising ID?
Where is my data stored, and who can read it?
Are there ads or ad SDKs in the app?
Is anything I write used to train AI models?
Can I export and delete everything myself, without writing to support?

Slate follows India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023. The full details are in the [privacy policy](/privacy/).

Two of the four promises we've made publicly are that Slate won't show you ads and won't sell or share your data.

pages.title: Calories on fasting days: Navratri, Ekadashi, Ramadan
pages.description: Fasting-day food like sabudana khichdi, kuttu puri and iftar snacks often has more calories than it looks. How to count it, with IFCT 2017 numbers.
pages.lede: On fasting days the food changes, not always the calories. Sabudana, kuttu, singhara, makhana, fried snacks and sweet milk are dense, so a Navratri plate or an iftar can come to more than an ordinary meal. Counting it works the same way as any other day.

content: Vrat food replaces wheat and rice with sabudana, kuttu (buckwheat), singhara (water chestnut) or rajgira, and it's often cooked in ghee with peanuts and potato:

ul: A plate of [sabudana khichdi](/calories/sabudana-khichdi/) made from 50 g of dry sabudana, with potato, peanuts and ghee, is about {{kcal@sabudana-khichdi:plate}} calories.
A [kuttu puri](/calories/kuttu-puri/) is about {{kcal@kuttu-puri:one}}, close to a wheat puri, because the frying oil is most of it.
A cup of plain [makhana](/calories/makhana/) is about {{kcal@makhana:cup}}, and 30 g roasted in a teaspoon of ghee about {{kcal@makhana:ghee30}}.
Fruit, curd, milk and sweets made with milk and sugar add up across the day.

content: On a vrat many families eat one full meal and snacks through the day, so the total depends on the whole day rather than any one plate.

On Ekadashi many families avoid grains and pulses, so the day's food is often potato, sabudana, milk, fruit and nuts. Potato sabzi in ghee, sabudana and peanuts are where most of the calories come from. A 200 ml katori of [aloo sabzi](/calories/aloo-sabzi/) is about {{kcal@aloo-sabzi:k200}}.

During Ramadan the day's food is eaten at sehri before dawn and iftar after sunset. Iftar often starts with dates and goes on to fried snacks such as samosas and pakoras, fruit chaat and sweet drinks. Dried dates have about 317 calories per 100 g, according to ICMR-NIN. A home [samosa](/calories/samosa/) is about {{kcal@samosa:one}} calories, and a glass of [nimbu pani](/calories/nimbu-pani/) with 2 teaspoons of sugar about {{kcal@nimbu-pani:two_tsp}}.

body.h2: How to count a fasting day

ol: Count each item as you would on any day: the plate, the katori, the piece.
Watch the ghee and the peanuts. They're the biggest part of most vrat dishes.
Count fried snacks by the piece and sweets separately.
Count drinks: sweet milk, lassi and sherbet carry sugar.

content: If you have diabetes, are pregnant, or take regular medication, talk to your doctor before a fast and about how to eat on fasting days. This page is about counting, not about whether to fast.

In Slate you can mark your fasting days, so it reads lines such as "sabudana khichdi" or "kuttu ki puri" the way you mean them. Each line gets its own number, worked out from IFCT 2017 values and recipes in grams. Slate never suggests a fast, a diet or a goal.

faq.q: How many calories are in a plate of sabudana khichdi?
faq.a: About {{kcal@sabudana-khichdi:plate}} for a plate made from 50 g of dry sabudana with potato, peanuts and a tablespoon of ghee.

faq.q: Are vrat foods lower in calories?
faq.a: Not usually. Sabudana, kuttu, peanuts, ghee and fried snacks are dense, so a fasting-day plate can have more calories than an ordinary meal.

faq.q: How many calories are in dates?
faq.a: Dried dates have about 317 calories per 100 g, according to ICMR-NIN. Fresh dates have less, about 144 per 100 g, because they hold more water.

faq.q: Should I count calories while fasting?
faq.a: That's your choice. If you have a medical condition or take medication, talk to your doctor about fasting. Slate counts what you write and never suggests a fast or a goal.

pages.title: Calories in office canteen food and tiffin
pages.description: How to count a canteen thali, a tiffin dabba and office chai: rotis, katoris of dal and sabzi, and the extra oil in canteen cooking, from IFCT 2017.
pages.h1: Calories in office canteen food and tiffin
pages.linkLabel: Calories in office canteen food and tiffin
pages.lede: Office food is the same few things most days: a canteen thali or a tiffin dabba, and several cups of chai or coffee. Count each of them once, carefully, and the rest of the week is quick.

content: A canteen thali is usually rotis, rice, dal, a sabzi, sometimes a sweet or curd. Canteen kitchens cook in large batches, often with more oil than home cooking, and the ladle sets the portion. Count it as outside food.

For a rough home baseline: two medium [rotis](/calories/roti/) are about {{kcal@roti:two}} calories, a 200 ml katori of [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/) about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}}, a katori of [mixed veg sabzi](/calories/mixed-veg/) about {{kcal@mixed-veg:k200}} and a 200 ml katori of [rice](/calories/plain-rice/) about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}}. Canteen versions of the dal and sabzi are usually higher.

A tiffin from home is easier to count, because you know what went in. Look at your dabba once: how many rotis or theplas, and how big the containers are. Measure a container the same way as a katori, with water and a measuring jug.

Common tiffin food travels well: [theplas](/calories/thepla/) at about {{kcal@thepla:one}} each, [aloo paratha](/calories/aloo-paratha/) at about {{kcal@aloo-paratha:one}}, [curd rice](/calories/curd-rice/) at about {{kcal@curd-rice:k200}} for a 200 ml katori, and [veg pulao](/calories/pulao/) at about {{kcal@pulao:k200}}.

Office chai is easy to forget. A cup of [masala chai](/calories/masala-chai/) with 2 teaspoons of sugar is about {{kcal@masala-chai:cup2}} calories, and a tumbler of [filter coffee](/calories/filter-coffee/) with whole milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar about {{kcal@filter-coffee:two_tsp}}. Three or four cups a day is a small meal's worth.
Canteen and vending-machine chai is often sweeter than home chai. Biscuits and namkeen with it add more.

body.h2: How to count office food quickly

ol: Count the canteen thali by its parts the first time, then reuse it.
Count your tiffin dabba once, by its containers.
Count chai by the cup, with the sugar you actually take.
Add the evening snack separately: samosa, vada pav, biscuits.

content: Tell Slate where you eat outside, including an office canteen and tiffin, and canteen food is counted as outside food, with more oil and a bigger portion than home food. Your chai and coffee are set once in Your kitchen, with your sugar and milk.

faq.a: About {{kcal@masala-chai:cup2}} for a cup with 2 teaspoons of sugar, and about {{kcal@masala-chai:cup0}} without sugar.

faq.a: Count it once by its contents: the rotis or theplas, and each container as a katori of dal, sabzi or rice. After that, the same dabba takes seconds.

pages.title: Why your katori size changes your calorie count
pages.description: A 250 ml katori holds two thirds more than a 150 ml one. How katori size changes the calories in dal, rice and sabzi, and how to measure yours.
pages.h1: Why your katori size changes your calorie count
pages.linkLabel: Why your katori size changes your calorie count
pages.lede: "One katori of dal" can mean 150 ml in one home and 250 ml in the next, and that alone changes the calories by two thirds. If you count Indian food by the katori, knowing the size of yours is the single most useful thing you can measure.
takeaways: Katoris in Indian homes are commonly 150, 200 or 250 ml. A 250 ml katori holds two thirds more than a 150 ml one.
A katori of rice weighs less than a katori of dal, because cooked rice is light and airy: about 0.67 g per ml against about 1 g for dal.
Measure your everyday katori once with water and a measuring jug, and count level katoris.
For dal, the most reliable count is the dry dal that went into the pot: ICMR-NIN's standard portion is 30 g.

content: There's no standard katori. Steel katoris sold in India come in many sizes, and families often use one size for dal and another for sabzi or dessert. On this site, every katori dish is shown at 150, 200 and 250 ml, the range most home katoris fall in.
Here's what that range does to some everyday dishes:

content: For one katori the gap looks small. Across a day, with two or three katoris at lunch and dinner, it adds up to the difference between a light meal and a full one.

body.h2: Why a katori of rice weighs less than a katori of dal
content: A katori measures volume, but calories follow weight. Cooked rice has air between the grains, so a 200 ml katori holds about 134 g of it. USDA lists a cup (236.6 ml) of cooked white rice at 158 g, which is about 0.67 g per ml. Thin dal is mostly water, so it's close to 1 g per ml, and a 200 ml katori holds about 200 g.

That's why a katori of [rice](/calories/plain-rice/) and a katori of [dal](/calories/dal-tadka/) can have quite different calories even though they look the same size. Rice is about {{per100@plain-rice}} calories per 100 g cooked, and thin dal tadka about {{per100@dal-tadka}}.

The figures above are for a level katori. A heaped katori of rice or sabzi can hold noticeably more, and rice pressed into a katori to make a neat mound holds more again. Dal and sambar can't be heaped, but they can be thick or thin.

Thickness matters as much as size for dal. A 200 ml katori of thin [dal tadka](/calories/dal-tadka/) is about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} calories, while the same katori of thicker [dal fry](/calories/dal-fry/) is about {{kcal@dal-fry:k200}}. The katori didn't change; what's in it did.

Many homes use a smaller katori for sabzi and dessert than for dal. Sabzis vary even more than dals: a 150 ml katori of [cabbage sabzi](/calories/cabbage-sabzi/) is about {{kcal@cabbage-sabzi:k150}} calories, while the same katori of [aloo sabzi](/calories/aloo-sabzi/) is about {{kcal@aloo-sabzi:k150}}, mostly because of the potato and the oil.
Dessert katoris matter because what goes in them is dense. Halwa, kheer and shrikhand carry far more calories per spoon than dal, so a small katori of dessert can hold as much as a big katori of dal.

ol: Take the katori you use most for dal or sabzi.
Fill it with water to the level you usually serve to, not to the brim.
Pour the water into a measuring jug, or weigh it on a kitchen scale: 1 g of water is 1 ml.
Round to the nearest of 150, 200 or 250 ml, and use that size from then on.

content: If you use a bigger bowl for one dish, such as a soup bowl for khichdi, measure that too. You only need to do this once.

body.h2: When the katori isn't the best unit
content: Some foods count better another way. Rotis, parathas and puris count by the piece, and their calories follow the atta in them: a [phulka](/calories/phulka/) from about 24 g of atta is about {{kcal@phulka:one}} calories, a medium [roti](/calories/roti/) from 30 g about {{kcal@roti:medium}}.

For dal, the most reliable unit is the dry dal that went into the pot. ICMR-NIN's standard portion of pulses is 30 g raw, about 100 calories ([Dietary Guidelines for Indians](https://nin.res.in/downloads/DietaryGuidelinesforNINwebsite.pdf), Annexure 14). However thin or thick the dal ends up, a bowl made from 30 g of dry [toor dal](/calories/toor-dal/) has about {{kcal@toor-dal:bowl}} calories before the tadka.

body.h2: Using your katori size in practice
content: Once you know your katori, keep to it: the same katori for dal every day makes your numbers comparable from one day to the next, even if no single number is exact. If you eat out, assume restaurant katoris and bowls are whatever size they look, and count the extra oil separately.
Slate asks for your katori once, in Your kitchen, as 150, 200 or 250 ml, and every home katori you write after that uses it. You can change it any time; past days stay as they were.

faq.q: What size is a standard katori?
faq.a: There's no single standard. Home katoris are commonly 150 to 250 ml. Measure yours once with water and a measuring jug.

faq.q: How many grams of rice are in a katori?
faq.a: About 134 g of cooked rice in a level 200 ml katori, using USDA's 158 g per cup for cooked white rice. That's about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}} calories.

faq.q: How many calories are in one katori of dal?
faq.a: About {{kcal@dal-tadka:k150}} to {{kcal@dal-tadka:k250}} for thin dal tadka, from a 150 ml to a 250 ml katori. Thick dal has more.

pages.title: Home dal vs restaurant dal: where the calories come from
pages.description: Why a katori of restaurant dal can have twice the calories of home dal: thickness, ghee, butter, cream and portion size, with numbers from IFCT 2017.
pages.h1: Home dal vs restaurant dal: where the extra calories come from
pages.lede: A katori of dal from a restaurant often has twice the calories of the same katori at home, sometimes more. The dal itself is much the same. The difference is how thick it is, how much ghee, butter and cream go in, and how big the serving is.
takeaways: A 200 ml katori of thin home dal tadka has about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} calories; a thicker restaurant dal tadka about {{outLo@dal-tadka}} to {{outHi@dal-tadka}}.
Thickness is the biggest hidden factor: a thick dal holds more dal and less water in every katori.
Each teaspoon of ghee or butter is about 35 to 45 calories, and restaurants often finish dal with more than one.
Dal makhani is a different dish altogether: about {{kcal@dal-makhani:k200}} for a home katori and {{outLo@dal-makhani}} to {{outHi@dal-makhani}} at a restaurant.

body.h2: How much is in a katori of home dal
content: Start with what's in an everyday home dal. A textbook dal tadka from Basic Food Preparation, a standard Indian cookery manual, uses 30 g of toor dal in 300 ml of water, with 10 g of ghee between the dal and the tadka. A 200 ml katori of it has about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} calories and {{protein@dal-tadka:k200}} g of protein.
Most of the calories in that katori come from two places in roughly equal parts: the dal and the ghee. That's useful to know, because they're also the two things a restaurant changes.

body.h2: Thickness: the difference you can't see on a menu
content: Home dal is often thin, poured over rice. Restaurant and dhaba dal is usually thicker, cooked down so it sits on a spoon. A thicker dal holds more dal and less water in every katori, so the same katori carries more calories even before any extra ghee.

When we compared a published restaurant-style dal tadka recipe with the textbook one, the fat per gram of dal was about the same. The difference per katori came mainly from thickness: restaurant dal at 1.5 to 2 times as thick gives about {{outLo@dal-tadka}} to {{outHi@dal-tadka}} calories in a 200 ml katori.

[Dal fry](/calories/dal-fry/) shows the same thing at home. With its onion-tomato masala cooked in and half the water, a 200 ml katori is about {{kcal@dal-fry:k200}} calories, against about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} for thin dal tadka.

body.h2: Ghee, butter and the second tadka
content: Fat is the other half of the story. A teaspoon of ghee is about 45 calories and a teaspoon of butter about 35, from IFCT 2017 and USDA values. Restaurants often add a second tadka right before serving, or a spoon of butter on top, and a dhaba dal fry may have its masala fried in more ghee than a home kitchen would use.
You can sometimes see it: a shine of ghee on top, a pool of butter melting in the centre. When you can't see it, assume there's more fat than at home rather than less.

[Dal makhani](/calories/dal-makhani/) is the richest dal on most menus. It's whole urad with a little rajma, simmered for hours and finished with butter and cream. A textbook home version, the Moti Mahal dal in The Art & Science of Cooking, comes to about {{kcal@dal-makhani:k200}} calories for a 200 ml katori.

Restaurant versions use much more of both. An open recipe in the Indian Nutrient Databank uses 3 tablespoons of butter and 2.5 of cream for 180 g of dal. A restaurant katori, finished with a teaspoon or two of butter and a swirl of cream, is about {{outLo@dal-makhani}} to {{outHi@dal-makhani}} calories.

A restaurant serving of dal isn't one katori by definition. Bowls and delivery containers vary, and many are meant for sharing. Counting what you actually ate, in your own katoris, matters as much as knowing the calories per katori.

body.h2: How to count dal when you eat out

ol: Count by katori, not by order. Estimate how many of your katoris the serving holds.
Use the restaurant range, not the home number. The middle of the range is a fair default.
Add visible fat: a spoon of butter or ghee on top is another 35 to 45 calories.
Treat dal makhani as its own dish, not as dal.
If you share, count your share.

content: None of these numbers is exact. A restaurant doesn't publish its recipe, and two dhabas on the same road will make different dal. The aim is a fair estimate you can repeat, not a precise one.

If you'd like restaurant dal closer to home dal, the levers are the same ones that raise it. Plain yellow dal or dal tadka usually carries less fat than dal fry, and dal fry less than dal makhani. Many restaurants will leave off the butter on top or the cream if you ask, and a second tadka is easy to skip. Each teaspoon of ghee or butter you leave out is about 35 to 45 calories.

In Slate, every line can be switched between Outside and Made at home. Outside food is counted with more oil and a bigger portion, so "dal tadka from Swiggy" and "1 katori dal" give different numbers, and you can tap either to see how it was worked out.

faq.q: Why does restaurant dal have more calories than home dal?
faq.a: Restaurant dal is usually thicker, finished with more ghee, butter or cream, and served in bigger portions. The dal itself is much the same.

faq.q: How many calories are in a katori of restaurant dal tadka?
faq.a: About {{outLo@dal-tadka}} to {{outHi@dal-tadka}} for a 200 ml katori, against about {{kcal@dal-tadka:k200}} for thin home dal tadka.

faq.q: How many calories are in restaurant dal makhani?
faq.a: About {{outLo@dal-makhani}} to {{outHi@dal-makhani}} for a 200 ml katori, depending on the butter and cream.

pages.title: Your chai over a day: what 3 or 4 cups add up to
pages.description: Four cups of chai a day with 2 teaspoons of sugar each come to about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} calories. What 2, 3, 4 and 5 cups add up to, with and without sugar.
pages.h1: Your chai over a day: what 3 or 4 cups add up to
pages.lede: Four cups of home chai a day, each with 50 ml of toned milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar, add up to about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} calories. The same four cups without sugar are about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup0}}. One cup is about {{kcal@masala-chai:cup2}}; the [masala chai page](/calories/masala-chai/) has the per-cup arithmetic. This post adds up the day: cups, spoons of sugar, milk and cutting chai.
takeaways: Four cups with 2 teaspoons of sugar each is about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} calories a day; without sugar, about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup0}}.
Sugar is the biggest part of the day's number: each level teaspoon is about 16 calories, so 2 teaspoons in 4 cups is 8 teaspoons, about 34 g.
Four cutting chais with a teaspoon of sugar each come to about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cutting}}, close to the {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup0}} of 4 full cups without sugar.
Buffalo milk raises the day: 4 cups with 50 ml of buffalo milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar each are about {{sum:4*masala-chai:buffalo}}.

body.h2: How many calories are in one cup of chai?
content: A cup of home masala chai with 50 ml of toned milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar has about {{kcal@masala-chai:cup2}} calories, about {{kcal@masala-chai:cup0}} without sugar, and a cutting chai with a teaspoon about {{kcal@masala-chai:cutting}}. ICMR-NIN's [Dietary Guidelines for Indians](https://nin.res.in/downloads/DietaryGuidelinesforNINwebsite.pdf) count a cup of tea with 50 ml of toned milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar at 75 calories, close to the same. The recipe, the milk and sugar options and the arithmetic are on the [masala chai calories](/calories/masala-chai/) page; everything below multiplies that cup by the day.

body.h2: How many calories are in 2, 3 or 4 cups of chai a day?
content: Most people don't stop at one: two cups at home, one at office and one in the evening is four. With 2 teaspoons of sugar each, that's about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} calories in the day from chai alone. With toned milk and 50 ml per cup:

table.caption: Total for the day, home chai with 50 ml of toned milk per cup.
head: Cups a day
No sugar
1 tsp sugar each
2 tsp sugar each

content: A large mug can be twice a cup, so count it as two. Instant chai premixes and sachets already contain sugar and milk solids, so count them by their label rather than as home chai.

body.h2: How much sugar is in your chai over a day?
content: A level teaspoon of sugar weighs about 4.2 g, according to USDA, and has about 16 calories. Two teaspoons in each of 4 cups is 8 level teaspoons, about 34 g of sugar: the difference between about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} for the day and about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup0}} without any. In many homes the sugar spoon is heaped, which puts more into every cup than these numbers assume. If yours is, count each teaspoon as a little more than a level one.
Dropping one teaspoon from every cup takes 4 cups from about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} to about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup1}}.

Jaggery and sugar are close per gram: IFCT 2017 puts jaggery at {{ing:jaggery}} calories per 100 g, and USDA puts white sugar at 387. Switching from one to the other changes the flavour more than the day's number.

body.h2: Does cutting chai change the day more than cutting the sugar?
content: A cutting chai at a tapri is half a glass, about half a cup, usually with a teaspoon of sugar. Four cutting chais come to about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cutting}} calories for the day, close to the {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup0}} of 4 full cups without sugar, and against about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} for 4 full cups with 2 teaspoons each. Halving the cup and dropping the sugar land in much the same place.

body.h2: What does the milk do over a day?
content: The milk sets the rest. Toned milk (3% fat) has about 58 calories per 100 ml, going by Amul Taaza's label. IFCT 2017 puts whole cow's milk at about 73 and buffalo milk at about 107. A cup with 50 ml of buffalo milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar is about {{kcal@masala-chai:buffalo}} calories, against about {{kcal@masala-chai:cup2}} with toned milk, so 4 cups of buffalo-milk chai come to about {{sum:4*masala-chai:buffalo}} for the day.

Milkier chai, made with half milk and half water or all milk, has more again. Each extra 100 ml of toned milk in a cup adds about 58 calories, so a day of doodh patti made almost entirely with milk can be several times a day of everyday chai. If you make chai with 100 ml of milk per cup, count the milk twice.

A tumbler of [filter coffee](/calories/filter-coffee/) with whole milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar is about {{kcal@filter-coffee:two_tsp}}, more than chai mostly because it has more milk, so a day of coffee adds up faster.

body.h2: What about tapri and station chai?
content: Chai from a tapri or a railway station is often sweeter and milkier than home chai, sometimes made with buffalo milk or condensed milk. We found no lab measurement of tapri chai, so as a range, assume up to a teaspoon more sugar and a little more full-fat milk: about {{outLo@masala-chai}} to {{outHi@masala-chai}} calories a cup. Over 3 or 4 cups the top of that range is well above the home figure, so count outside cups at the top of it unless you know the stall.
Biscuits, rusk and namkeen with chai are counted separately, and often add more than the chai itself.

body.h2: What adds nothing over the day?
content: Tea leaves, a longer boil for a kadak cup, grated ginger, crushed cardamom and chai masala add almost nothing, however many cups you have. Lemon tea and black tea without sugar are close to zero. Green tea without sugar is the same.

body.h2: How do you count chai without thinking about it?
content: Chai is easy to forget because it's small and frequent. The simplest habit is to decide what your usual cup is, with your milk and your sugar, and count each cup as that. In Slate, your chai and coffee are set once in Your kitchen, with sugar in teaspoons and milk as none, toned or full fat, and "chai" on a line uses them.

faq.q: How many calories are in 4 cups of chai a day?
faq.a: About {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} with 50 ml of toned milk and 2 teaspoons of sugar in each cup, about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup1}} with 1 teaspoon, and about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup0}} without sugar.

faq.q: How many calories are in 3 cups of chai a day?
faq.a: About {{sum:3*masala-chai:cup2}} with 2 teaspoons of sugar in each cup, about {{sum:3*masala-chai:cup1}} with 1 teaspoon, and about {{sum:3*masala-chai:cup0}} without sugar, for home chai with toned milk.

faq.q: How many calories are in 5 cups of chai a day?
faq.a: About {{sum:5*masala-chai:cup2}} with 2 teaspoons of sugar in each cup, and about {{sum:5*masala-chai:cup0}} without sugar.

faq.q: How much sugar is in my chai over a day?
faq.a: Count the teaspoons. Two level teaspoons in each of 4 cups is 8 teaspoons, about 34 g of sugar at about 16 calories each. A heaped teaspoon holds more.

faq.q: Does cutting chai have fewer calories over a day?
faq.a: Yes. Four cutting chais with a teaspoon of sugar each come to about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cutting}}, against about {{sum:4*masala-chai:cup2}} for 4 full cups with 2 teaspoons each.

pages.title: How to count calories in a thali without weighing anything
pages.description: Count a thali by its pieces and katoris: rotis, dal, rice, sabzi, farsan and sweets. Worked examples for a Gujarati, a Punjabi and a South Indian thali.
pages.h1: How to count calories in a thali without weighing anything
pages.linkLabel: How to count calories in a thali
pages.lede: You don't need a scale to count a thali. Count the pieces (rotis, puris, papad, sweets), count the katoris (dal, sabzi, kadhi, rice), and add the ghee you can see. That gets you a fair estimate.
takeaways: Break the thali into pieces and katoris, and count each one.
Rotis and rice are usually the biggest part of the total; sweets and fried farsan add the most per bite.
Count every refill as another katori or another roti.
Ghee poured at the table is about 45 calories a teaspoon and easy to miss.

content: A thali looks complicated because it has many small things on it. Counted one by one, it's simple:

ol: Pieces: rotis, puris, theplas, papad, farsan, sweets. Count how many.
Katoris: dal, kadhi, sabzi, raita, kheer. Count how many, and how full.
Rice: count it in katoris too. A 200 ml katori of [plain rice](/calories/plain-rice/) is about {{kcal@plain-rice:k200}} calories.
Fat you can see: ghee on the rice or dal, butter on a roti. About 45 calories a teaspoon for ghee.
Refills: every extra roti or katori is another one.

content: If the thali's katoris are smaller or bigger than yours at home, count them as a fraction of yours.
A Gujarati thali usually has rotlis, dal, bhaat, a shaak, kadhi, a farsan such as dhokla, and a sweet. As home values:

table.caption: Home values. Restaurant thalis usually have more ghee and more refills.
head: Item
About
rows: Gujarati [toor dal](/calories/toor-dal/), a bowl from 30 g dry dal

content: A Punjabi thali often has roti or naan, dal makhani, a paneer dish, rice and raita. Made at home it comes to about this; restaurant versions carry more butter and cream, so use the restaurant ranges on each page if you ate out:

table.caption: Home values. A restaurant thali is usually well above this.
head: Item
About

content: Swap the rotis for one large restaurant [butter naan](/calories/butter-naan/), about {{kcal@butter-naan:large}}, and the total rises by about 400 calories on its own.
A South Indian meals plate is rice-based: rice with sambar, rasam, a poriyal, curd and papad, often with refills of rice and sambar. As home values:

table.caption: Home values. Sambar varies a lot with thickness and coconut.
head: Item
About

content: Rice is most of it, so the rice refills are the thing to count carefully here. A thinner everyday sambar without coconut has about half the calories per katori.

The same thali from a restaurant is usually higher, for the same reasons restaurant food usually is: more ghee, butter and cream, and refills that keep coming. In a restaurant, a 200 ml katori of [dal makhani](/calories/dal-makhani/) is about {{outLo@dal-makhani}} to {{outHi@dal-makhani}} calories, against about {{kcal@dal-makhani:k200}} at home, and a restaurant serving of [paneer butter masala](/calories/paneer-butter-masala/) is about {{outLo@paneer-butter-masala}} to {{outHi@paneer-butter-masala}}, against about {{kcal@paneer-butter-masala:bowl}} for a home bowl.
Wedding and festival thalis add more fried food and more sweets, and a buffet makes the portions harder to see. Counting pieces and katoris works for those too.

The small things on the side are easy to skip, and some of them add up. ICMR-NIN's [Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2011)](https://nin.res.in/downloads/DietaryGuidelinesforNINwebsite.pdf) count 2 tablespoons of coconut, groundnut or til chutney at about 120 calories and a tablespoon of tamarind chutney with jaggery at about 60, while a tablespoon of tomato chutney is about 10. Pickles in oil carry the oil, and a fried papad carries the oil it was fried in.

ul: Ghee on the rice and dal, poured at the table.
Fried farsan: a home [samosa](/calories/samosa/) is about {{kcal@samosa:one}} calories, a [kachori](/calories/kachori/) about {{kcal@kachori:one}}.
Puris instead of rotis: four home [puris](/calories/puri/) are about {{kcal@puri:four}}.
Sweets: a [gulab jamun](/calories/gulab-jamun/) is about {{kcal@gulab-jamun:one}}, a piece of [kaju katli](/calories/kaju-katli/) about {{kcal@kaju-katli:shop}}.
Refills of rice and roti, which are easy to stop counting.

body.h2: How exact this needs to be
content: A thali counted this way gives an estimate. Most restaurants don't publish their recipes, and every home cooks differently, so counting the same way each time is what makes your numbers comparable from one week to the next.
In Slate you can write a thali as one line, "4 rotli, dal, bhaat, shaak, kadhi", and each item gets its own line and its own number, using your katori and roti sizes for home food.

faq.q: How many calories are in a Gujarati thali?
faq.a: About {{sum:phulka:four+toor-dal:gujarati+plain-rice:k150+cabbage-sabzi:k150+kadhi:k150+dhokla:two+gulab-jamun:one}} for a home thali with 4 small rotlis, dal, rice, sabzi, kadhi, 2 pieces of dhokla and a gulab jamun. Restaurant thalis with refills and ghee are usually more.

faq.q: Can I count a thali without weighing?
faq.a: Yes. Count the pieces and the katoris, add the ghee you can see, and count every refill.

faq.q: What's the highest-calorie part of a thali?
faq.a: Usually whatever you eat most of: the rotis, the rice or a rich curry such as paneer butter masala. Per bite, sweets and fried farsan add the most.

faq.q: How many calories are in a South Indian meals plate?
faq.a: About {{sum:2*plain-rice:k200+sambar:k150+rasam:k150+cabbage-sabzi:k150}} for two 200 ml katoris of rice with sambar, rasam and poriyal at home, before curd, papad and refills.

faq.q: How much does ghee on rice add?
faq.a: About 45 calories for each teaspoon. Two spoons poured over rice and dal at the table is about 90.

pages.title: Counting calories on fasting days without stress
pages.description: Navratri, Ekadashi and Ramadan food is often more filling in calories than it looks. A calm way to count it, and when it's fine not to count at all.
pages.h1: Counting calories on fasting days without stress
pages.lede: Fasting days change what you eat, and sometimes when, but counting them doesn't have to be harder than any other day. Count the few things you eat the same way you always do, accept rough numbers, and stop counting for the day if it's getting in the way.
takeaways: Vrat food is often dense: a plate of sabudana khichdi is about {{kcal@sabudana-khichdi:plate}} calories, mostly from sabudana, peanuts and ghee.
Kuttu and singhara puris have about the same calories as wheat puris; the frying oil is half of it.
At iftar, dates, fried snacks and sweet drinks add up quickly.
Rough numbers are fine. If counting on a fasting day adds stress, it's fine to skip it.

body.h2: Why fasting days feel harder to count
content: Fasting days break the usual pattern. Meals move to different times, familiar dishes are replaced with vrat food, and there's often more fried food and sweets than on an ordinary day. Many people also find that thinking hard about food on a religious or family occasion feels out of place.
None of that changes how counting works. A plate is still a plate, a puri is still a puri, and the same rough method that works on other days works here.
Navratri and other vrat days swap wheat and rice for sabudana, kuttu, singhara and rajgira, and the cooking often uses ghee and peanuts:

ul: A plate of [sabudana khichdi](/calories/sabudana-khichdi/) made from 50 g of dry sabudana is about {{kcal@sabudana-khichdi:plate}} calories. The peanuts and ghee are close to half of that.

A [kuttu puri](/calories/kuttu-puri/) is about {{kcal@kuttu-puri:one}}, close to a wheat [puri](/calories/puri/) at about {{kcal@puri:one}}, because the oil taken up in frying is most of the difference between a puri and a roti.
A 200 ml katori of [aloo sabzi](/calories/aloo-sabzi/) is about {{kcal@aloo-sabzi:k200}}.
A cup of plain [makhana](/calories/makhana/) is only about {{kcal@makhana:cup}}, because it's light; roasted in ghee it's more.

content: On Ekadashi many families avoid grains and pulses, so potato, sabudana, milk, fruit and nuts make up the day. The same numbers apply.

During Ramadan the day's food is eaten at sehri before dawn and iftar after sunset. Iftar often begins with dates, then fried snacks, fruit and sweet drinks. Dried dates have about 317 calories per 100 g, according to ICMR-NIN's [Dietary Guidelines for Indians (2011)](https://nin.res.in/downloads/DietaryGuidelinesforNINwebsite.pdf). A home [samosa](/calories/samosa/) is about {{kcal@samosa:one}} calories, and a glass of [nimbu pani](/calories/nimbu-pani/) with 2 teaspoons of sugar about {{kcal@nimbu-pani:two_tsp}}.
If you count, count the iftar plate the way you'd count a thali: the pieces, the katoris and the glasses.

body.h2: Sweets and drinks on festival days
content: Fasting days are often festival days too, with sweets and sweet drinks shared at home and at the temple. A home [gulab jamun](/calories/gulab-jamun/) is about {{kcal@gulab-jamun:one}} calories, a [besan ladoo](/calories/besan-ladoo/) about {{kcal@besan-ladoo:one}}, and a glass of [sweet lassi](/calories/lassi/) about {{kcal@lassi:glass}}.
Counting one or two of these isn't hard. It's the ones eaten in passing, a piece here and a ladoo there, that are easy to lose track of.

body.h2: What a vrat day can add up to
content: As an illustration rather than a plan: a plate of sabudana khichdi, two kuttu puris with a 200 ml katori of aloo sabzi, and a glass of sweet lassi come to about {{sum:sabudana-khichdi:plate+2*kuttu-puri:one+aloo-sabzi:k200+lassi:glass}} calories. That's before fruit, tea, makhana or sweets.
The total will be different in every home. What it shows is that a fasting day often isn't lighter than an ordinary one, and knowing that can make the numbers less surprising.

body.h2: A calm way to count a fasting day

ol: Write down what you eat as you eat it, in plain words: "sabudana khichdi, 1 plate", "2 kuttu puri", "1 glass lassi".
Use the same portions every time. Your plate of sabudana khichdi is one plate, whatever it weighs.
Don't chase exact numbers. A range is honest, and fasting-day food varies a lot from home to home.
Look at the week, not the day. One festival meal doesn't change much on its own.

content: Counting is a tool, and it's fine to put it down. If counting on a fasting day makes the day feel worse, or takes away from the occasion, skip it and pick it up again the next day.

If you have diabetes, are pregnant, or take regular medication, talk to your doctor before fasting and about what to eat on fasting days. And if your relationship with food feels hard, or counting starts to feel like pressure, talk to someone. In India, Tele-MANAS is free and available any time on 14416.

In Slate you can mark your fasting days so it reads lines like "kuttu ki puri" the way you mean them. Slate never suggests a fast, a diet or a goal. If you'd rather keep writing but not see numbers for a while, Hide calorie counts removes every calorie number from the app; the macros stay.

faq.q: How many calories are in sabudana khichdi?
faq.a: About {{kcal@sabudana-khichdi:plate}} for a plate made from 50 g of dry sabudana with potato, peanuts and ghee.

faq.q: Is vrat food lower in calories?
faq.a: Usually not. Sabudana, kuttu, peanuts, ghee and fried snacks are dense, so a vrat plate can have more calories than an ordinary meal.

faq.q: Should I count calories while fasting?
faq.a: Only if it helps you. It's fine to skip counting on a fasting day. If you have a medical condition, talk to your doctor about fasting.

faq.q: How many calories are in a kuttu puri?
faq.a: About {{kcal@kuttu-puri:one}} for a home kuttu puri made with about 13 g of buckwheat flour, so four are about {{kcal@kuttu-puri:four}}.

faq.q: How many calories are in dates at iftar?
faq.a: Dried dates have about 317 calories per 100 g and fresh dates about 144, according to ICMR-NIN. How many you eat decides the rest.

pages.title: What "maintenance calories" means, and how to measure yours
pages.description: Maintenance calories are what your body uses in a day. How formulas estimate it, why they're only a starting point, and how to measure yours from a log.
pages.h1: What "maintenance calories" really means, and how to measure yours
pages.lede: Maintenance calories are the calories your body uses in a typical day: what you'd need to eat for your weight to stay where it is. Formulas can estimate it, but the only way to know your own is to measure it, from what you eat and how your weight moves over a few weeks.
takeaways: Maintenance calories are your total daily energy use: your body at rest, plus movement, plus digesting food.
Formulas such as Mifflin-St Jeor estimate the resting part from weight, height, age and sex; an activity factor adds the rest.
Formulas are averages, and your own maintenance can differ from them.
Measured maintenance comes from a few weeks of honest logging alongside a weight trend.
It's a measurement, not a target.

content: Your body uses energy all day. Most of it goes to keeping you alive at rest: breathing, circulation, keeping warm, the work of every organ. That's your resting energy use, often called BMR (basal metabolic rate) or REE (resting energy expenditure). On top of that comes everything you do, from walking to the bus to exercise, and a smaller amount used to digest food.

Add those together for a typical day and you get your total energy use, which is what people mean by maintenance calories. If you eat about that many calories on average, your weight stays about the same. For what typical Indian dishes add, see [Calories in Indian food](/calories/).

A widely used formula for resting energy use is the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, published in the [American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 1990](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2305711/) from measurements of 498 adults:

ul: Men: 10 x weight in kg + 6.25 x height in cm - 5 x age + 5
Women: 10 x weight in kg + 6.25 x height in cm - 5 x age - 161

content: To get from resting energy to a whole day, it's multiplied by a physical activity level (PAL). The FAO, WHO and UNU's report on [human energy requirements](https://www.fao.org/4/y5686e/y5686e07.htm) classes a sedentary or lightly active lifestyle at a PAL of 1.40 to 1.69, an active or moderately active one at 1.70 to 1.99, and a vigorously active one at 2.00 to 2.40.

Take a woman aged 30, 160 cm tall and 60 kg: 10 x 60 + 6.25 x 160 - 5 x 30 - 161 = 1,289 calories at rest. With a desk job and little other movement, a PAL of 1.40 to 1.69 puts her maintenance at roughly 1,800 to 2,180 calories a day.
For a man aged 30, 175 cm and 75 kg: 10 x 75 + 6.25 x 175 - 5 x 30 + 5 = 1,699 calories at rest, and roughly 2,380 to 2,870 a day at the same activity level.

body.h2: Why a formula is only a starting point
content: Formulas describe averages. In the original study, weight, height, age and sex together explained about 71% of the differences in measured resting energy use between people. The rest came from things the formula can't see, such as how much of your weight is muscle.

The activity factor is a wider guess still. Two people with desk jobs can move very differently through the day. So a formula gets you into the right area, and for some people it's well off in either direction.

The way to know your own maintenance is to measure it. If you log what you eat honestly and your weight trend stays flat, your average intake is about your maintenance. If the trend drifts up or down, your maintenance is below or above what you've been eating. Turning the speed of that drift into calories needs a few weeks of data, and it's the arithmetic Slate Plus does for you, described below.

ol: Log everything you eat and drink for at least three weeks, as consistently as you can. Rough numbers are fine if you count the same way each day, though if you always undercount, the measured number comes out low by about the same amount. The [home cooking](/for/home-cooking/) guide covers counting dal, roti and oil.
Weigh yourself a few times a week, at the same time of day.
Look at the trend, not single weigh-ins. Water, salt and meal timing move the scale from one day to the next; a smoothed trend line shows the direction.
Compare your average daily intake with the direction of the trend.

content: Weight also takes a long time to settle after a lasting change in eating. A 2011 analysis in [The Lancet](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3880593/) put the half-time of the body's response at about a year. So a few weeks of trend shows the direction you're moving in, not where your weight will end up.
Maintenance describes what your body has been doing. What you do with that number is up to you.

If you have a medical condition, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are under 18, energy needs work differently and the formulas above don't apply in the same way. Talk to a doctor or a registered dietitian.

Slate shows your BMR and sedentary baseline for free, from your age, sex, height and weight, and updates them as your weight trend changes. With Slate Plus, after about three weeks of logging and a few weigh-ins, Slate works out how many calories your body has actually been using each day from what you logged and how your weight trend moved. It shows it as a measurement and doesn't turn it into a goal or a suggestion.

faq.q: What are maintenance calories?
faq.a: The calories your body uses in a typical day, at rest and moving. Eating about that many on average keeps your weight about the same.

faq.q: How do I calculate my maintenance calories?
faq.a: A formula such as Mifflin-St Jeor estimates your resting energy use, and multiplying by an activity level (1.40 to 1.69 for a sedentary or light lifestyle, from FAO, WHO and UNU) gives a starting estimate. Measuring it from a few weeks of logging and a weight trend is more accurate.

faq.q: Is BMR the same as maintenance?
faq.a: No. BMR is what your body uses at rest. Maintenance adds movement and digestion on top, so it's higher.

pages.lede: One piece of a Diwali sweet is between about {{kcal@kaju-katli:shop}} calories (a 10 g kaju katli) and about {{kcal@gulab-jamun:one}} (a gulab jamun), with most pieces, a soan papdi cube, a peda, a motichoor ladoo, landing between {{kcal@soan-papdi:one}} and {{kcal@motichoor-ladoo:one}}. body.h2: How many calories are in one piece of each Diwali sweet?
content: Every row is a home or sweet-shop piece of the size named, drained of syrup where there is syrup, with the page's own number. The pages explain the recipe, where each value comes from and how it compares with lab analyses and packed labels.

content: The two columns tell different stories. A gulab jamun tops the per-piece list because it is the biggest piece, soaked in syrup; per 100 g it is in the middle. Kaju katli and soan papdi are the richest per gram, because they are mostly nuts, ghee and sugar with almost no water, but a shop cuts them small.

body.h2: How many calories are in a box of Diwali sweets?
content: Boxes are sold by weight, so use the per 100 g column. A 500 g box of kaju katli is about {{sum:5*kaju-katli:g100}} calories, about 50 pieces of 10 g. A 250 g box of soan papdi is about {{kcal@soan-papdi:g250}}, about 12 cubes. A 500 g box of motichoor ladoo is about {{sum:5*motichoor-ladoo:g100}}, around 18 ladoos of 28 g. Half a kilo of peda is about {{sum:5*peda:g100}}.

A box is rarely eaten by one person in one sitting, and the number that matters for your day is the pieces you took. Two pieces of kaju katli and a soan papdi cube come to about {{sum:2*kaju-katli:shop+soan-papdi:one}}. The [meal calculator](/calories/calculator/) adds up a plate of mixed sweets typed in plain words, such as "2 kaju katli, 1 motichoor ladoo, 1 gulab jamun".

body.h2: Which Diwali sweets have the fewest calories per piece?
content: By the piece, the smallest pieces: a 10 g kaju katli at about {{kcal@kaju-katli:shop}}, a small 13 g packed peda at about {{kcal@peda:small}}, a rasgulla drained of its syrup at about {{kcal@rasgulla:one}}, and a jalebi at about {{kcal@jalebi:one}}. A 21 g soan papdi cube is about {{kcal@soan-papdi:one}}.

By weight, the sweets with the most water in them: rasgulla at about {{kcal@rasgulla:g100}} per 100 g, kheer at about {{kcal@kheer:g100}}, rasmalai with its milk at about {{kcal@rasmalai:g100}}. Syrup sweets drop further if you lift them out and let the syrup run off: a tablespoon of syrup on a gulab jamun is about 45 calories, which is the difference between {{kcal@gulab-jamun:one}} and {{kcal@gulab-jamun:one_syrup}}.
Sugar-free and low-sugar sweets made with sweeteners can be much lower than any of these; count them from the packet's label, not from these pages.

body.h2: How many calories are in Diwali snacks like chakli and mathri?
content: The savoury side of the faral plate is richer per gram than the sweets, because fried snacks are dry and hold oil. Per 100 g: [mathri](/calories/mathri/) about {{kcal@mathri:g100}}, [namak para](/calories/namak-para/) about {{kcal@namak-para:g100}}, [shakarpara](/calories/shakarpara/) about {{kcal@shakarpara:g100}}, [chakli](/calories/chakli/) about {{kcal@chakli:g100}}. For comparison, a [samosa](/calories/samosa/) is about {{kcal@samosa:one}} a piece and a [khasta kachori](/calories/kachori/) about {{kcal@kachori:one}}.

content: A piece of chakli or a few namak para is small. A small bowl of chakli, about 50 g, is about {{kcal@chakli:bowl}}, and that is the portion that disappears with a cup of chai.

Dry-fruit boxes are the other Diwali gift, and nuts are dense: IFCT 2017 puts cashews at about {{ing:cashew}} calories per 100 g and almonds at about {{ing:almond}}. A 25 g handful is a quarter of that, in the same range as a sweet-shop piece of kaju katli, which is itself half cashew. Raisins are about {{ing:raisins}} per 100 g. Count dry fruit by the handful the way you count sweets by the piece.

body.h2: How do you count sweets across the Diwali days?
content: Diwali is five days, from Dhanteras to Bhai Dooj, and sweets arrive at every one of them. The simplest way to count is by the piece, at the time you eat it, with the piece's size: a kaju katli is a kaju katli, a big wedding ladoo is a big one. Write the pieces on the day's line and let the total take care of itself; a day with four sweets on it is a day with four sweets on it, and the next day starts at zero.

The [meal calculator](/calories/calculator/) counts a line like "2 kaju katli, 1 motichoor ladoo" with these numbers, and "half kaju katli" or "1 big motichoor ladoo" changes the size. A sweet from a halwai or a box can be bigger than the home piece; the pages above give the shop sizes where they differ.
If a festival week turns into something that worries you about food, the number is not the thing to fix. Talk to someone you trust, or to a doctor or dietitian; Tele-MANAS (14416) is free, any time.

faq.a: About {{kcal@kaju-katli:shop}} for a 10 g sweet-shop piece, and about {{kcal@kaju-katli:one}} for a bigger home piece. Half a shop piece is about 25.

faq.q: How many calories are in one motichoor ladoo?
